title: What law is (ST I-II.90.4)
hook: an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community

segments.voice: Yesterday, charity is friendship: good will both ways, built on the happiness God shares. Your line was friendship with god. What true thing did you say, and to whom? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

A red light, very late at night. No cars in any direction. No camera, no police, nobody on the sidewalk. The light stays red, and a driver sits there anyway, drumming on the wheel, feeling slightly ridiculous. Why wait? Out of fear? Out of habit? Or because the rule is actually for something? Thomas Aquinas wanted to know what makes a rule a law at all, and not just somebody's order with a penalty attached. He packed his answer into one sentence, and that sentence is today.
screen: `A RED LIGHT, NOBODY AROUND.` → `WHY WAIT?` → `WHAT MAKES A RULE A LAW?`

segments.voice: Here's Thomas's sentence, in plain English. Law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community, and made known. Take it a piece at a time. First, reason. A law isn't just a strong will. Thomas says that if a ruler's command isn't measured by reason, it's closer to wrongdoing than to law. A law is a kind of thinking: it points actions toward an end. Second, the common good. A law aims at the good of the whole community, not one person's private advantage, not even the lawmaker's. Third, the one who has care of the community. Not just anyone gets to make law; it belongs to the whole people, or to someone who stands in for them and looks after them. Fourth, it has to be made known. A law nobody could ever learn binds nobody. And that last piece has a lovely turn: Thomas says the deepest law, the natural law, was made known when God placed it in human minds. Now the edge of the sentence. If a rule fails the test, if it serves the ruler against the people, Thomas says it's more like violence than law. He doesn't say every such rule may be ignored on the spot; sometimes, he says, it's wiser to bear it than to cause greater harm. But it isn't law in the full sense. Scripture puts wisdom behind good law. In Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims, wisdom speaks: "By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things." So for Thomas, law isn't the enemy of freedom. A good law is reason, handed to a community, so that people can live well together.
screen: `AN ORDINANCE OF REASON.` · `FOR THE COMMON GOOD.` · `BY THE ONE WHO CARES FOR THE COMMUNITY.` · `AND MADE KNOWN.` · then, large: `LAWGIVERS DECREE JUST THINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: obey one good rule gladly. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind a rule you follow most days without thinking: a speed limit, a house rule, a workplace policy, a line at the coffee shop. Run it through Thomas's sentence. Is it reasonable? Whose good does it serve? Who made it, and how did you learn it? If it passes, notice what it protects: someone's safety, someone's time, a little peace. Then choose to keep it today on purpose, not grudgingly, as a small gift to the people it protects. The bell holds the time.
What law is. For Thomas, an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community, and made known. Today's word.
Your line: reason for the common good. Today, when a rule annoys you, ask what it's for and whom it serves before you decide what to think of it. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Catholic social teaching draws on Thomas's account of law and the common good, and the Catechism teaches that authority is legitimate when it seeks the common good by morally acceptable means.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: law pertains to reason, and a ruler's will not regulated by reason 'would savor of lawlessness rather than of law' (I-II.90.1 ad 3); the common good (90.2); the whole people or one who has care of them (90.3); promulgation, with the natural law promulgated by God's instilling it into human minds (90.4 ad 1); unjust laws as 'acts of violence rather than laws', which may sometimes be obeyed to avoid scandal or disturbance (96.4).
The trapdoor counts four articles (q. 90, aa. 1–4); confirm.
